weller_1.speaker: weller
weller_1.text: Finally. A little longer and I'd have come to pick you up myself for the second time tonight. You look: almost human. Progress, I'd say.

weller_2.speaker: weller
weller_2.text: Crawford, I found you in a bar last night looking so bad the bartender was thinking ambulance, not taxi. Do you even remember how you got home?

anna_2.speaker: anna
anna_2.text: Vaguely. I remember the shower. I remember the coffee was terrible.

weller_3.speaker: weller
weller_3.text: The coffee was fine. You were terrible. I spent two hours bringing you back. Shower, coffee, more coffee, then you went out for a smoke and came back looking a little more like a living person. You know what would happen to any other detective in this department after the third time in a month?

anna_3.speaker: anna
anna_3.text: Let me guess. A talk with the mentor, then HR, then a farewell party with a badge-shaped cake.

weller_4.speaker: weller
weller_4.text: They wouldn't be here anymore, Anna. At all. They keep you because you're: Never mind. Just. This can't go on forever. I'm not going to lecture you every morning for the rest of my career. Just: one day I might not be around to pull you out of a bar before someone sees it who won't care that you're the best detective in the department.

choices.text: Then try to be around more often, Weller. You're clearly good at it.
I'm fine. Really. Just a rough week.
I know. I'm sorry. Really sorry - for last night, and for the fact that this clearly won't be the last time.

after_1.speaker: anna
after_1.text: By the way. Do I at least not smell? Be honest, because if someone with a dog's nose walks into the interrogation room right now:

after_2.speaker: weller
after_2.text: A little. But luckily most of our suspects come in smelling so bad they'd cover anything. Mint gum on the desk, by the way - I left it for you. Don't thank me.

after_3.speaker: anna
after_3.text: I won't. All right - tell me what we've got.

after_4.speaker: weller
after_4.text: Edward Scolfield. Former military, forty-three. Twenty years of service, retired three years ago. Wife - Tamara, stepson - Greg, fifteen. The relationship between them was: let's say not a relationship but a cold war. Neighbors heard shouting regularly. Tamara never called the police - the classic picture. Alibi - full of holes. The camera by the garage caught him leaving a few minutes after the estimated time of death. Apparently he thought the time gap would be written off as forensic error. It won't be.
